passage: I remember the night before my scholarship interview. My cousin Yamini poked her head in and said, brightly, "Relax, Ramesh, it will be fine!" and went back to her show. I felt something close inside me. Nobody had asked what I was afraid of. I nodded and said okay, but I stopped practising for an hour. Two weeks later, before my driving test, she sat next to me and said the same three words, quietly, after asking what worried me most. That time they helped. It made me see the words are not the thing; the tone and whether she wanted to hear me are. I wonder if she even noticed the difference.

qa.q: When was Yamini's bright "it will be fine"?
qa.a: It was the night before Ramesh's scholarship interview.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh feel something close inside when Yamini said it?
qa.a: Ramesh felt she was not taking the fear seriously, since she did not ask what Ramesh was afraid of and went back to her show. Ramesh still nodded politely, so it was not obvious to her.

qa.q: What could Yamini do next time to make her comfort land better?
qa.a: Ask what worries Ramesh first, sit close and say the words quietly, as she did before the driving test.

qa.q: How might Yamini have seen her own remark that night?
qa.a: She may have thought she was cheering Ramesh up and had no idea it felt hollow.

grounding: The same words of reassurance comfort or dismiss depending on tone and timing.

passage: Counsellor's note, Friday. Suraj told me that after his maths exam he said he was afraid he had failed. His mother replied quickly, "Don't be silly, it will be fine," while packing his lunchbox. He nodded, but he told me the words felt like a door closing. He was not looking for a promise, he said, just for someone to ask which question troubled him. He also said his uncle's "It will be fine" felt good last month, because his uncle sat with him first and asked what happened. We talked about how he can say, "Can you listen first?" I have suggested he try telling his mother that. Naveen.

qa.q: What was Suraj's mother doing when she said it would be fine?
qa.a: She was packing his lunchbox.

qa.q: What did Suraj seem to want when he told his mother he might have failed?
qa.a: He seems to want someone to ask which question troubled him and to listen before comforting him. The words felt to him like a door closing.

qa.q: What could Suraj try with his mother?
qa.a: He could tell her plainly, "Can you listen first?" so she knows what helps him.

qa.q: How might Suraj's mother feel about his reaction?
qa.a: She may be surprised, since she meant to comfort him and did not intend to dismiss him.

grounding: Reassurance such as it will be fine can feel hollow to a teen depending on timing and tone.

passage:
Thursday night
Results tomorrow. At tuition Chandrika bounced up and said, "It will be fine, yaar! You always panic for nothing!" and went back to her phone. She meant well, I know. But it felt like being patted on the head. Like my worry was a silly thing to wave off. I said "yeah" and stared at the whiteboard for an hour.
Then tonight Mummy found me sitting on the stairs. She didn't say anything at first. She sat down one step below and asked, "Which paper is scaring you?"
"Physics," I said, and told her about question six.
She listened to the whole thing. Then she said, very quietly, "It will be fine. And if it isn't, we'll work it out together."
Same words as Chandrika's. Completely different. I'm going to sleep now.
- Akash

qa.q: Which paper was scaring Akash?
qa.a: Physics was the paper scaring Akash, especially question six.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling after Chandrika's cheerful "It will be fine"?
qa.a: Akash felt dismissed and a little hurt, as if the worry were silly, which is why the reply was just "yeah" and an hour of staring at the whiteboard.

qa.q: Why did Mummy's version of the same words work better?
qa.a: She listened first and spoke quietly, and added that they would work it out together, so the reassurance came after Akash felt taken seriously.

qa.q: How might Chandrika have seen her own words?
qa.a: Chandrika probably thought she was cheering Akash up and had no idea the quick, bright tone came across as brushing the worry aside.

grounding: The diary shows the same reassuring words feeling dismissive in one tone and timing and comforting in another.

qa.q: Which part of the first day worried Tejas most?
qa.a: Lunch worried Tejas most, standing there with a tray and nowhere to sit.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when replying "you always say that"?

qa.q: What did Payal change that made the chat go better?
qa.a: Payal stopped cheering, asked what the worst part was, said it sounded awful, and offered a concrete plan for lunch.

passage:
The monsoon flood had come into Jatin's grandfather's shop in Sehore on Sunday night. By Monday morning the sacks of rice and dal on the lowest shelves were ruined, and Jatin had spent five hours helping carry out wet stock before school.
In class, Dilnaz Ma'am saw his muddy shoes. "Oh, the flood? It will be fine, these things happen every year." She turned to the board.
Jatin's face closed. He put his head down on the desk.
At break Dilnaz Ma'am noticed he hadn't moved. She came and sat on the bench next to his.
"I said that too fast," she said. "Tell me what happened."
He told her about the sacks, and his grandfather sitting silently in the wet shop.
"That sounds really hard for your family," she said. "It may take time. The school can give you extra days on the project, and I'll ask about help for the shop."

qa.q: How many hours had Jatin spent helping carry out wet stock?
qa.a: Jatin had spent five hours helping carry out wet stock before school.

qa.q: What did Jatin's head on the desk suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggested he felt dismissed and upset that his family's loss was brushed off, though it could also have been plain exhaustion after five hours of work.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz Ma'am do at break that worked better?
qa.a: She admitted she had spoken too fast, asked him to tell what happened, named how hard it was, and offered real help instead of quick cheer.

qa.q: How might Jatin's grandfather have heard "these things happen every year"?
qa.a: He would likely have heard it as his loss being treated as small, since he was sitting silently in his ruined shop.

grounding: The scene shows "It will be fine" sounding dismissive when said too quickly, and a teacher repairing it by listening.

passage: On the night before her chemistry resit, Nour sat at the kitchen table in their Manchester flat, highlighter uncapped, staring at the same page she had been on for an hour. Siddiq passed with his toast and said, "You'll be fine, habibti. Honestly. It'll be fine." Nour slammed the book shut. "You don't know that. You didn't even ask what I'm stuck on." Siddiq stopped, toast halfway to his mouth. He had meant it as a hug in words. He pulled out a chair. "Okay. What are you stuck on?" "Titrations. All of it." They went through two questions together, badly, laughing at his rusty memory and a calculator that kept rolling off the table. At eleven, when she finally closed the book, he said it again, softer: "It'll be fine." This time she leaned her head on his shoulder for a second. "Yeah," she said. "Maybe it will."

qa.q: What was Nour revising for?
qa.a: Nour was revising for her chemistry resit.

qa.q: Why did Nour slam the book shut?
qa.a: Nour felt anxious and dismissed: 'It'll be fine' came before anyone asked what she was stuck on, so it sounded like her worry wasn't taken seriously. She may also have been tired and frustrated with the page.

qa.q: What made the same words comfort her at eleven?
qa.a: By then Siddiq had sat down and worked through the problem with her, so 'It'll be fine' came after real attention and in a softer tone.

qa.q: How did Siddiq mean the first 'It'll be fine'?
qa.a: Siddiq meant it as a hug in words, so he was surprised when Nour heard it as being brushed off.

grounding: It shows the same reassuring words feeling dismissive when rushed and comforting after real listening, depending on tone and timing.
